books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1861. Public domain. Wording verified against the Teaching American History text (teachingamericanhistory.org/document/first-inaugural-address-6/) and the Senate document (govinfo.gov, S. Doc. 62-439). The two passages appear in this order in the address; '. . .' marks omitted text.
stimulus.text:
Apprehension seems to exist among the people of the Southern States that by the accession of a Republican Administration their property and their peace and personal security are to be endangered. There has never been any reasonable cause for such apprehension. . . . I do but quote from one of those speeches when I declare that “I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so.”

. . .

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The Government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors. . . . We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained, it must not break our bonds of affection. The mystic chords of memory . . . will yet swell the chorus of the Union, when again touched, as surely they will be, by the better angels of our nature.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The two passages together best support which conclusion about Lincoln's strategy in March 1861?

options.text: Lincoln planned to free the slaves in the seceded states at once.
options.misconception: The first passage promises the opposite: no interference with slavery where it exists.

options.text: Lincoln accepted secession as lawful and final.
options.misconception: Background: elsewhere in the address Lincoln calls the Union perpetual and secession ordinances legally void.

options.text: Lincoln offered to let the seceded states keep federal forts.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln pledged to hold federal property, and Fort Sumter was the fort at issue.

options.text: Lincoln paired reassurance on slavery with resolve to hold the Union.

rationales.A: The first passage promises the opposite: no interference with slavery where it exists.
rationales.B: Background: elsewhere in the address Lincoln calls the Union perpetual and secession ordinances legally void.
rationales.C: Background: Lincoln pledged to hold federal property, and Fort Sumter was the fort at issue.
rationales.D: The first passage reassures the South on slavery where it exists, while the second warns that war comes only if the South starts it. Background: the address holds both halves at once — conciliation on slavery, no surrender on the Union.
rationales.general:
1. The first passage soothes: slavery where it exists will not be touched.
2. The second passage warns: the Government will not strike first, but the choice is the South's.
3. Background: Lincoln was speaking to two audiences, Southerners he hoped to calm and Northerners he needed to hold.
4. Reassurance plus resolve was the whole strategy.
Remember: a speech can offer peace with one hand and draw a line with the other; track both hands.
